summary:
Same-sex conduct between adults is lawful in Madagascar only from age 21. Article 331 of the Penal Code treats same-sex acts involving a person under 21 as indecent assault, with a reported penalty band of five to ten years' imprisonment; the record also carries a two-to-five-year penalty for "indecent or against nature" acts. The age of consent is unequal, so a trans visitor whose partner or counterparty is under 21 carries a criminal exposure that a heterosexual visitor does not.

Marriage is closed to same-sex couples, and no recognition of civil unions is provided. Article 2 of Law No. 2007-022 on Marriage and Matrimonial Regimes prohibits marriage between two persons of the same sex whether before the Civil Registrar or under traditional ceremonies. Article 39 of the same law names "gender identity" as a cause for absolute nullity of marriage, a direct legal exposure for a trans person whose marriage is challenged.

In a 2020 case a 33-year-old woman was arrested for the statutory rape of a 19-year-old woman after the younger woman's mother filed a complaint; the mother was allegedly acting to cover an incest and rape accusation against the father. Religious leaders offered the younger woman conversion therapy during the proceedings.

Public expression is constrained. In early July 2021 the Malagasy government cancelled an LGBTQ party held at a bar in Antananarivo on the grounds of "incitement to debauchery". A France 24 report of August 2024 found that although homosexuality is not illegal, it is socially unacceptable to a degree that many LGBT people hide their sexuality to keep their jobs and live in peace, developing their own networks and coded language.

The most recent documented finding of violence against gender-nonconforming people in this record is the 2011 US State Department Human Rights Report, which recorded public attitudes ranging from tacit acceptance to violent rejection, particularly of transgender sex workers, who were frequent targets of verbal abuse, stone throwing and even murder. That report covered a post-coup period in which it also documented unlawful killings and societal discrimination and violence against the LGBT community. No later instance of anti-trans violence is documented in this record. One further incident is undated in the source: supporters of a same-sex couple were subjected to insults and death threats on social media, and religious leaders publicly accused them of "promising homosexuality".

At Madagascar's fourth Universal Periodic Review in January 2025, out of 235 recommendations, the government rejected UN recommendations to combat anti-LGBT violence and hate speech and to equalise the age of consent. Six Malagasy organisations, Queer Place, Mifoha Olo Mazoto, Divers' Unité, Justice Égalitaire, Men Engage and Madagascar LGBT+, responded that "Refusing to act is to endorse impunity and condone violence."

Health protection is framed through HIV policy rather than trans-specific care. Act No. 2005-040 on the Fight against HIV/AIDS requires information, education and communication programs adapted to the sexual orientation of target groups, and Article 26 mandates special provisions to protect vulnerable groups, expressly including young people, sex workers, men who have sex with men and mobile populations, against HIV transmission.

Two statutes limit disclosure of a visitor's status. Law No. 2014-038 on the Protection of Personal Data, Article 18, bars processing of sensitive data including data on health or sexual life, and Law No. 2017-045 on Credit Information Bureaus, Article 2, likewise protects sexual orientation as sensitive data.
tangentialFactors:
Madagascar's position sits within a wider regional movement. A BBC News Pidgin overview of July 2020 recorded that roughly 22 of 53 African states had moved to decriminalise same-sex conduct, while listing Madagascar as legal only from age 21 with no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions. The comparison is one of direction, not of parity: Madagascar retains an unequal age of consent that the states which fully decriminalised have removed.

A guide updated 3 December 2023 by Queer in the World assesses Madagascar's legal framework as limited in progress compared with other countries, with LGBT people facing discrimination and lacking civic rights such as marriage and adoption. The assessment is a comparative judgement by a advocacy publication rather than a legal finding.

The 2011 US State Department report must be read against the post-coup regime it describes, in which it documented unlawful killings alongside societal discrimination and violence. Rights in Exile lists state-protection capacity, case law and supporting organisations among the areas its Madagascar resources cover, which indicates that protection machinery and case law are documented elsewhere rather than in this record.
localsOnly:
Family formation is restricted to heterosexual married couples. Article 33 of Law No. 2005-014 on Adoption states that "Full adoption is only permitted to heterosexual spouses," and most civic liberties, including the rights to marry and adopt children, are not afforded to LGBTQ individuals.

Residents manage the social climate through concealment. The France 24 report of August 2024 describes LGBT Malagasy hiding their sexuality to keep jobs and live in peace, and maintaining their own networks and coded language.

Domestic organisations engage the review mechanism directly. The six groups that protested the January 2025 UPR position are Queer Place, Mifoha Olo Mazoto, Divers' Unité, Justice Égalitaire, Men Engage and Madagascar LGBT+.

Two statutes govern data controllers handling sensitive personal information: Law No. 2014-038 on the Protection of Personal Data, Article 18, bars processing of sensitive data including data on health or sexual life, and Law No. 2017-045 on Credit Information Bureaus, Article 2, protects sexual orientation as sensitive data.

Public-health obligations run to resident populations. Act No. 2005-040 on the Fight against HIV/AIDS requires information, education and communication programs adapted to the sexual orientation of target groups, and Article 26 mandates special provisions protecting young people, sex workers, men who have sex with men and mobile populations against HIV transmission.
outOfScopeNotes:
Not sourced in this inventory: legal gender recognition, passport and identity-document gender markers, visa and entry requirements, and any airport or border screening practice affecting trans or gender-nonconforming travellers. No claim is made either way on these points.

The date of the incident in which supporters of a same-sex couple received insults and death threats on social media is not given in the source, so it cannot be placed in the record's timeline.

No trans-specific violence figure with a denominator exists for Madagascar in this inventory, and no per-capita comparison with the general homicide rate can be made. The violence findings available are the 2011 US State Department reporting and the 2020 statutory rape case; no later documented instance of anti-trans violence appears here.

Unresolved: the outcome of the 2020 case, and whether the conversion therapy offered to the 19-year-old woman was taken up or acted on, are not documented. The specific UPR recommendations rejected in January 2025 are reported only in three categories, not itemised. No case law applying Article 39's gender-identity ground of nullity is included in this record.
